articles.title_orig: Taiwan’s elections not about China, but Beijing has a lot to say
articles.title_zh: Taiwan’s elections not about China, but Beijing has a lot to say
articles.content_orig:
By Ben Blanchard and Yimou Lee
TAIPEI, Nov 24 (Reuters) – Taiwan’s mayoral and county chief elections on Saturday are not directly about China, but the ruling party’s nomination for Taipei mayor — a lawmaker wanted by Chinese police for “separatism” — has sent Beijing into a flurry of denunciations.
China, which views Taiwan as its own territory but does not govern the democratic island, ​says the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei candidate Puma Shen is a “traitor” who is playing up the China threat to ‌trick people into voting for him.
In October, Taipei prosecutors indicted four people for putting monitoring devices on a scooter parked outside Shen’s home, issuing arrest warrants for two people from Hong Kong it said were behind the scheme.
The same month, China’s main state broadcaster CCTV said Shen was “deceptively” seeking votes by “playing the oppose China card” and using “little tricks” by talking about external interference in the election.
China last month imposed sanctions on his father’s business in China, adding to those already on Shen.
Taipei ‌has ​repeatedly accused Beijing of stepping up operations ahead of local elections including military activity, cyberattacks ⁠and information warfare.
“For years, the Chinese Communist Party ⁠has tied its Taiwan policy to the outcome of Taiwan’s elections, making pre-election interference inevitable,” Taiwan’s top China policy maker, Chiu Chui-cheng, told Reuters.
Such interference “will only backfire and deepen resentment among the people of Taiwan toward the Chinese Communist regime,” said Chiu, who heads the Mainland Affairs Council.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment. It has long rejected accusations it interferes ​in Taiwanese elections.
Shen himself has not made China a major focus of his campaign, instead concentrating on issues like urban renewal.
The DPP has only run Taipei once before, under Chen Shui-bian from 1994 to 1998. He later went on to become the DPP’s first ⁠president of Taiwan.
Shen has attracted a passionate support base known as the “Ocean Current,” ⁠initially driven by voters concerned about China and later strengthened by Shen’s policy-heavy campaigning, in which he described ​in detail what he would do if he won.
His opponent, incumbent mayor Chiang Wan-an, is from the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT), which traditionally ​favours close ties with China. Its chairwoman, Cheng Li-wun, met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing earlier this ‌year.
Chiang is well-known to China thanks to the annual Taipei-Shanghai city forum. He also has largely held off talking about relations with China during the campaign, focusing on issues like water safety and how under his leadership Nvidia signed a deal to build a new headquarters in Taipei.
‘DIEHARD TAIWAN INDEPENDENCE SEPARATIST’
Two senior DPP officials told Reuters that Shen had tapped into a sense of pro-Taiwan identity and become a symbol of defiance ⁠against China — to the surprise of many, even within his own party.
“He has awakened a renewed pro-Taiwan spirit,” said one of the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Shen was put on the list of obstinate “Taiwan independence” separatists by China’s Taiwan Affairs Office in October, 2024, which ⁠also sanctioned the Kuma Academy he co-founded, which ‌runs civil defence courses to prepare people to deal with a possible attack from Beijing.
China’s Taiwan ⁠Affairs Office last year called him a “diehard Taiwan independence separatist in every sense of the word”, ​saying people like ‌him are “traitors to the Chinese nation and criminals”.
Shen told Reuters earlier this month that China did ​not like his ⁠previous work about trying to bring greater global attention to disinformation.
“We try to tell other countries, hey, you need to be aware of this Chinese influence operation in your country,” he said.
Chiang’s campaign team said he did not have time to accept an interview.
It previously told Reuters that “no outside force should exert political pressure on Taiwan’s democratic elections” and it opposed any “domestic or outside forces that use any means to intervene in, interfere with, or influence voters’ voting intentions”.
Reporting on opinion polls is banned by law in the 10 days before the election.
(Reporting by Ben Blanchard and ​Yimou Lee; Editing by Raju Gopalakrishnan)

articles.title_orig: Trump administration blacklists Megaspeed, key firm in Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: Trump administration blacklists Megaspeed, key firm in Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. has added Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other Southeast Asian companies to its trade blacklist, citing national security and foreign policy concerns.
The Department of Commerce in a Federal Register filing cited a "significant risk" of companies being or becoming involved in diverting advanced computing products to unauthorized end users or end uses.
The blacklisting comes as Jensen Huang returns to the helm of Nvidia following his departure amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is under investigation by U.S. authorities.
Megaspeed International is a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that operates data centers across Southeast Asia.
The restrictions apply to all items subject to U.S. Export Administration Regulations, with license applications to be reviewed under a "presumption of denial."
The blacklist also includes PT Megaspeed International and MSFusion Sdn. Bhd. in Malaysia, as well as Megaspeed (Thailand) Co., Ltd. The filing identified 7Road International as an alias used by both Megaspeed's Singapore and Thailand entities.
The Commerce Department initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations after identifying suspicious activity through its monitoring of potential semiconductor diversion, according to a join statement issued with the Justice Department.
In May 2025, Commerce Department investigators requested records from Nvidia regarding direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list the following month, according to the statement.
U.S. authorities, working with Singaporean law enforcement officials, also conducted an on-site end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed its then-CEO Alice Huang. The Justice Department subsequently took the lead in the criminal investigation into the company.
Commerce also added an Alibaba subsidiary in Singapore, Apex Enterprise Solutions, to a trade blacklist, Reuters reported.
Alibaba said it would pursue all legal avenues to protect its rights and reputation, adding that Apex had never diverted advanced computing chips subject to U.S. export restrictions, according to Reuters.
Meanwhile, Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said at a news conference in Canberra, Australia, on Tuesday that investigations into Megaspeed were ongoing and that discussions with American authorities were continuing.
"We do not want Singapore to be used and abused as a conduit by companies to circumvent America's export controls," Wong said.

articles.title_zh: Stock futures inch higher as traders see whether Nvidia can extend rally from Jensen Huang’s return: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures were slightly higher Monday evening after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO sent the chipmaker's shares soaring and sparked a rebound in the artificial intelligence trade.
Futures tied to the Nasdaq-100 futures were marginally higher. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures advanced 91 points, or 0.2%, while S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%.
In Asia, the Taiwan Weighted Index was up over 9%, with key chip stocks TSMC and Hon Hai Precision Industry closing in on their 10% price limits.
South Korea's Kospi jumped over 7% on Tuesday, with heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix seeing gains of about 8% and 10% respectively.
Japan's Nikkei 225 also rose 4.45%, also powered by chip related stocks, and Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was also up 1.78%.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was up 1.05%, while mainland China's CSI 300 was flat in early trade.
Nvidia surged 31% during Monday's regular session, leading a rally in chip stocks. The Nasdaq Composite closed 6.5% higher, the S&P 500 finished up 4.7% and the Dow Industrials rose 3% Monday.
It was the best session for the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 since April 9, 2025 when President Donald Trump announced a reprieve on tariffs.
The tech sector of the S&P 500 soared 9%, powered by sharp gains in semiconductors, memory names and neoclouds. Advanced Micro Devices added almost 7%, while Micron Technology surged 19%. Neocloud stock CoreWeave jumped 22%.
The market action was a sharp reversal from Friday's steep sell-off, which saw the S&P 500 and Dow close in correction as the AI trade suffered and Nvidia tanked.
"The shocking decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO helps to remove a key level of uncertainty from the AI trade, which has been suffering in recent weeks," said Glen Smith, chief investment officer at GDS Wealth Management. "Stock market corrections can sometimes end as quickly as they begin and we believe the bottom in stocks is likely in," he added.
Looking ahead to Tuesday's session, on the economic front, consumer confidence data is set to be released.

Key Nvidia partners and suppliers in Asia saw their shares skyrocket on Tuesday as investors piled back into the tech market, following the reinstatement of the company's CEO Jensen Huang by its board.
Taiwan's TSMC, a critical partner to the U.S. chip giant, surged almost 10%, while Hon Hai Precision Industry — known also as Foxconn — rose by a similar amount. Nvidia partner Mediatek also jumped 10%.
In South Korea, Nvidia suppliers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix climbed 8% and 10% respectively.The two companies, which together make up for more than 40% of the Kospi's weighting, helped send the index up over 7%.
Japan also saw gains among semiconductor related stocks, with Softbank Group , Advantest and Tokyo Electron climbing as the Nikkei 225 up almost 4%.
The chip giant's shares soared in Monday's session – and so did options activity for the stock.
More than 11 million options contracts traded on Nvidia Monday for the most active single day of trading for the stock's options.
Most of the options activity had a bullish tilt to it, with just under 6.7 million calls traded, compared to 4.3 million puts, according to Cboe LiveVol data.
Calls give the investor the right to buy shares at a stated price by a certain date, while puts give the investor the right to sell shares at a set price by an expiration date.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was also up 1.3%.

The group — which includes Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta Platforms, Nvidia and Tesla — added an aggregate $1.65 trillion in market cap on the session's moves.

articles.content_orig:
Nintendo's GameCube title Wave Race: Blue Storm has today made a splash on the Switch Online + Expansion Pack service.
If you have an active subscription and access to a Switch 2, you can play it right now via the 'Nintendo Classics' GameCube app. Here's Nintendo's official description:
"Storm warning! Prepare to ride the waves! Take to the water in this watercraft-racing game, released for the Nintendo GameCube™ system in 2001. Compete in contests of speed and technique—either racing against your rivals or going up against your own records. As you race across the waves, you can see the skies changes from calm and sunny to surging storms... Weather conditions can affect visibility, water levels, and the height of the waves over the course of a race, so you'll need to be prepared for whatever comes!"
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
This jet ski racer was a follow-up to Wave Race 64 (also available on the Nintendo Classics service) and arrived in 2001/02.
The game's water and weather effects were a stunning showcase on Nintendo's new hardware at the time, and the water physics in the title also raised the bar. Japan has received the same title on the Nintendo Classics service this week.
Alongside this latest game update ( Version 2.2.0 ), you can now also turn off the "border graphic" when playing GameCube titles. However, the player icon remains on the screen.

articles.title_orig: Iran Update, November 23, 2026
articles.title_zh: Iran Update, November 23, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Several major developments unfolded in Iran and across the region over the past month:
The Regime: Blockade, Energy Shortages, and the Risk of Unrest
The figures point to a gradual deterioration in conditions inside Iran. Household purchasing power declined further in late October. Reports of sharp disagreements at the top of the regime followed. By mid-November, shortages of gas and fuel had already triggered protests. The Iranian regime appears to be struggling to meet basic energy and subsistence needs.
Reuters reported on October 28, 2026, that Iranian households were cutting spending on food, housing, healthcare, and education as the war, blockade, and sanctions took their toll on the economy.
Reports also pointed to a rift between the regime’s political leadership and the IRGC. President Masoud Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lead the political camp. Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei and IRGC Commander Ahmad Vahidi represent the IRGC’s position. According to several reports, Rezaei and Vahidi are directing the regime’s wartime decisions on behalf of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
On November 10, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said the daily natural gas shortfall was expected to reach 430 million cubic meters this winter, compared with 300 million in previous winters. National Iranian Gas Company CEO Saeed Tavakoli said four major gas processing facilities were damaged in the opening stages of the war. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) reportedly released figures showing that the blockade had prevented $30 billion in oil exports since July 2026 and that 150 vessels had been diverted after attempting to export Iranian oil.
Iran International reported a five-kilometer queue at gas stations in the Kerman area. Fuel shortages also reportedly sparked protests and roadblocks in Bandar Abbas.
The Nuclear Program: Pickaxe Mountain, Isfahan (ENTC), and Monitoring Gaps
The focus of the nuclear discussion has recently shifted from access to the sites to the whereabouts of the uranium. In October, reports focused on the sealing of Pickaxe Mountain and U.S. threats to strike it. In November, attention shifted to enriched uranium outside the scope of monitoring and to an IAEA report saying the agency did not even know where the enrichment facility in Isfahan was located.
Reports on Pickaxe Mountain (Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La) describe a site that appears sealed from the outside, yet where activity and construction continue. The site has also become a focus of direct threats between Washington and Tehran. It is a deeply buried facility south of the Natanz complex.
Reuters reported on October 16, 2026, that Trump warned that the United States might have to strike the site. The following day, the Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS), headed by David Albright, published satellite images dated October 7. The images showed that the eastern tunnel entrances remained sealed with earth and that earthen barriers on the roads to the western entrances were still in place. The institute said this reinforced its assessment that access to the complex had been blocked for more than two months.
Nevertheless, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said construction had been observed at the site. In late October, ISIS published an elevation profile showing differences in elevation between the eastern and western tunnel entrances and the ventilation shafts. The institute said these differences could indicate several levels, two separate tunnels, or a descending western tunnel.
In early November, Trump told Fox News: “We eliminated their nuclear program. We have one or two facilities left to deal with. We might have to strike Pickaxe Mountain, but it’s not a big deal. We can do it in ten minutes or in an hour.” On November 11, Rezaei, who was appointed secretary of the Supreme National Security Council in August 2026, responded in an interview with Al Mayadeen. He said that if the site were attacked, Iran would strike distant U.S. bases, including bases in Europe. He added: “We will not allow a single grain of enriched material to leave Iran,” and said Iran needed the material to design nuclear-powered ships and submarines.
According to a November 14, 2026, report in Gulf Daily News, the IAEA confirmed activity at Pickaxe Mountain but said it had no information about what was taking place inside.
In November, attention shifted to Isfahan. The central question was where Iran’s enriched uranium was and why the IAEA could not verify its whereabouts. An agency report confirmed the extent of the monitoring gap.
Estimates differed as to the location of 440 kg of enriched uranium, with Pickaxe Mountain and the underground facility at the Isfahan Nuclear Technology Center (ENTC) among the possibilities. The IAEA assessed that at least half of the material remained buried in Isfahan after the first war with Iran, while other assessments suggested that some had been moved to Pickaxe Mountain.
The Isfahan facility is about 150 meters underground and has four entrances. The entrances were hit by U.S. Navy cruise missiles at the end of Operation Rising Lion, which began on June 13, 2025. They were not hit during Operation Roaring Lion, which began on February 28, 2026.
On November 9, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said IAEA inspectors had recently visited the Bushehr nuclear power plant, but that the visit did not signal broader access to nuclear sites. Iran submitted a ten-page document to the IAEA arguing that it was not obliged to allow full inspections while it remained under threat of attack.
In its November quarterly report, the IAEA said it did not know the location or status of the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP), or whether it contained nuclear material. International media reported on November 13, 2026, that Iran had declared the facility in June 2025 but had never allowed inspectors to visit it. The agency assessed that it was located deep inside an Isfahan tunnel complex bombed in June 2025. The reporting also noted that in March 2026 Grossi had assessed that a significant share of Iran’s uranium enriched to near weapons grade was stored in that complex.
Other Sites and the Enrichment Target
Beyond Pickaxe Mountain and Isfahan, satellite images documented reconstruction at other sites damaged in strikes, including sites ISIS links to the nuclear program. In November, a public statement from Tehran also called for the ability to enrich uranium to a higher level.
In October, ISIS documented repairs to what it assessed was probably a water tank, construction of a new support building, and increased vehicle activity at the Minzadehi nuclear site on the outskirts of Tehran, following Israeli strikes there in March 2026. The institute also published images of a second phase of reconstruction at Taleghan 2 in the Parchin complex. The Israeli Air Force struck the site in October 2024. According to the institute, it had previously been linked to explosives tests for nuclear weapon initiation mechanisms.
In early November, the BBC reported that new construction and excavation had been identified near tunnel entrances outside Qom, close to the Fordow enrichment facility. On November 8, Mohammad Javad Larijani, head of Iran’s Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences and an adviser to the supreme leader, said Iran needed the capability to enrich uranium to 80%.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive / Commerce adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist
articles.title_zh: Exclusive / Commerce adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist
articles.content_orig:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Easter Egg Opens a Portal to the Original 2002 Vice City
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Easter Egg Opens a Portal to the Original 2002 Vice City
articles.content_orig:
A YouTuber has uncovered the wildest GTA 6 Easter egg yet. Following a series of arcane clues and pulling a set of switches in the correct order sees players transported back to the 1980s.
Warning! Spoilers for GTA 6 follow.
The Easter egg begins in the R&D tower in Key Lento, GTA 6’s starting area, but spans almost the entire map. Players have to pull a series of switches and press certain buttons to trigger a portal into the past, complete with new voice acting from Danny Dyer as Kent Paul.
After scaling the tower, the YouTuber ( Memeio ) noticed that a sound effect from GTA Vice City plays when he messed with the lever and button. A poster for LPL (Leonida Power and Light) in the room then guided him around Leonida to the LPL power substations dotted around the map.
Each substation contained letters written on its walls. Memeio was so committed to figuring out the mystery that he actually followed the power cables across the map to track them all down.
After putting all the letters together from all 12 substations, Memeio realized they spelled out an interesting phrase: “Life is passing me by.” That phrase was a cheat code in Vice City that sped up the in-game clock.
On PlayStation, the code for that cheat was: Circle, L1, Square, L1, Square, L1, Triangle, Circle, Triangle.
Memeio realized that he had to enter that code using all the buttons and switches at the various substations, applying a button to different lever flips and button presses. After pressing the buttons in order, without fast travelling, Memeio got an in-game text to head to Reactor 2 between 7pm and 6am. When he did, a portal opened.
Stepping through the portal transported him to Vice City’s Malibu Club, complete with polygonal graphics. Upstairs, he even saw Kent Paul, voiced by British actor Danny Dyer, reprising his role. Danny Dyer is included in the credits for GTA 6 under the “local population" category.
For all that effort, you get access to Tommy Vercetti’s iconic floral shirt and his classic Malibu bike, complete with star decals.

articles.title_zh: Amazon drone delivering shampoo snags on wire and tumbles onto Michigan man’s garage roof
articles.content_orig:
When James Brennan was waiting for his shampoo delivery last week, he didn’t realize an Amazon drone would hit a wire and tumble onto the roof of his garage.
Brennan, of Huntington Woods, Michigan, near Detroit, said he had not requested a drone delivery and assumed his package would arrive at his doorstep as usual. But on Friday, he received a notification from Amazon telling him to keep an eye out for the unmanned aircraft, so he went outside to take a video.
“I just thought it would make amusing, amusing conversation over Thanksgiving or at work or whatever,” Brennan said in an interview. “And I was just going to get a shot of it. I never expected this to happen.”
He went to the front yard and heard the unmistakable whirling of a drone as it neared. The rotors kicked up leaves, debris and dust, Brennan said, before the drone set the package down and began its ascent again.
Video taken from across the street shows the drone hitting a cable, wobbling and ultimately plopping down on Brennan’s roof.
“It swayed a couple of times, and then it swayed over the top of the garage,” Brennan said. “It kind of laid down and died. And as soon as it laid down, the motors shut off, and that was it.”
Amazon workers responded to the incident quickly and retrieved the problem drone, but the ordeal did cause neighbors to temporarily lose internet access, he said.
In a statement, Amazon spokesperson Jack Stelzner said safety is the company’s “top priority” and that “incidents are extremely rare.”
“Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service,” he said.
A spokesman for the National Transportation Safety Board said officials are gathering information and have not decided whether to launch an investigation.
Brennan said the damage to his garage roof was “very minor,” comprising only a few scuffed shingles. He said he and some neighbors also got a $100 Amazon gift card for their troubles.
Brennan now hopes Amazon will continue to refine its drone delivery system to prevent future accidents.
“Until they develop better technology to spot these these kinds of things, this is going to continue to happen,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Japan’s Takaichi isolated on world stage
articles.title_zh: Japan’s Takaichi isolated on world stage
articles.content_orig:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a cold shoulder from China during the recent Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the tech hub of Shenzhen.
After Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen on November 18 for the two-day summit, there was an immediate issue when the mobile stairs to the door of her aircraft were some way short of the threshold, requiring her to hold on to the door frame to step down around 40 centimeters (about 15 inches) to the top step.
It may have been completely inadvertent, but upon safely reaching the airport tarmac, her official welcome was decidedly low-key. There were no musical performances, no cheering crowds or traditional dances, which were laid on for many other APEC leaders as they arrived.
Japan's Yomiuri newspaper reported on November 20 that when Takaichi met Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the dinner reception, "his reaction was cold." And while many other regional leaders managed at least a brief one-on-one with Xi on the sidelines of the main event, the Japanese delegation was not granted such access.
"The level of frostiness from the Chinese side was on full display from the moment Takaichi's plane landed," said William Yang, a Taiwan-based analyst for the International Crisis Group.
"I cannot think that the issue with the plane steps was anything other than deliberate and there was a huge contrast between the welcome she received and virtually everyone else," he told DW.
Yang added that the ice didn't break when Takaichi tried to speak to Xi at the dinner reception and the entire occasion "just reflects the state of bilateral relations."
China and Japan share a troubled history, marked by the Japanese invasion of China in the 1930s and the often brutal occupation of cities that were captured and subjugated.
Chinese schoolchildren learn about the horrors of the Nanjing Massacre and the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japanese forces.
Japan maintains that its repeated post-war apologies and massive economic aid that helped China to become the economic powerhouse it is today are overlooked amid the criticism.
Diplomatic relations were normalized in 1972 and Tokyo pursued a policy of engagement over the following decades, although that came to a halt in the mid-2000s, points out David Adebahr, a professor of international relations and Asia-Pacific security policy at Kobe University.

"China's rising military spending, the breakdown of talks over the East China Sea in 2006, and a resurgence of nationalism raised concerns even among Japan's more China-friendly diplomats, while defence analysts noted an increase in Chinese submarine activity near Japanese waters," he told DW.
The nationalism on display during the 2008 Beijing Olympics, coupled with China's more assertive stance over the Senkaku Islands, which Japan has sovereignty over but which Beijing claims, accelerated this shift.
Ties took a sudden nosedive in November 2025 when Takaichi responded to a question in Japan's parliament, the Diet, by saying that any "contingency” involving Taiwan would also inevitably threaten the national security of Japan.
According to Adebahr, the Japanese leader was merely saying out loud what "had long been the internal logic of Japanese security planning." Nevertheless, Beijing has reacted with fury .
China has demanded that Takaichi retract the statement and raised pressure on Japan by restricting exports of rare earth minerals critical to Japanese industry, banning imports of Japanese seafood and telling tourists to take Japan off their destination list.
And while ruffled national feelings have been smoothed in the past with shows of reciprocal goodwill, China is standing firm on its demands this time.
"From Tokyo's perspective, it is clear that Beijing believes it holds more cards than in the past," said Adebahr.
"Today, Beijing has considerable leverage: Japan's dependence on Chinese rare earths; an increasingly visible military presence around Japan, sometimes in conjunction with Russia; and a US administration that has urged Tokyo to de-escalate rather than firmly backing it."
Adebahr added that this left China with little incentive to offer Takaichi a face-saving compromise. However, he pointed out that Beijing's reliance on coercion could backfire by prompting Japan to increase defence spending and seek closer ties with other partners.
Still, the Japanese leader finds herself in a difficult position, said analyst Yang.
As a committed conservative who has talked tough on Beijing's rapid military buildup, its seizure of islands and atolls in the South China Sea and the inexorable pressure on Taiwan to capitulate and become one with mainland China, Takaichi cannot give in to Xi's demands for fear of losing face with her hardline base.
"This is a major test of her abilities and wisdom as the nation's leader," Yang said. "She is walking a political tightrope between reducing tensions with China but, at the same time, preparing the nation and its allies for a potential contingency over Taiwan."
"I foresee China maintaining its current approach, continuing to step up the pressure by limiting targeted exports and amplifying the assertion with Russia and North Korea that Japan is embracing remilitarization," he said.
Yang added that Japan was likely to seek opportunities to signal goodwill and improve relations "in return for small-scale compromises." However, he said that a reset in the dynamics would depend on how the Trump administration shaped its foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.
Analyst Adebahr said that while he expects diplomatic relations to remain frosty, there are too many interdependencies for a full decoupling between China and Japan.
"I would not be too pessimistic about the relationship, because in the medium term, trade, technology and critical minerals are now seen as security issues," he added. "Therefore, complex interdependence will prevent a return to the old pattern of keeping politics and economics separate."
"While economic interdependence alone will not be enough to stabilize the relationship, full decoupling is highly unlikely, as transaction costs would be far too high for both sides," he said.

articles.title_orig: Congress is going to war with Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Congress is going to war with Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Members of Congress responded with swift, bipartisan fury Monday over the Nvidia board's surprise decision to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang at the behest of President Donald Trump, opening a new phase of questions about the chipmaking giant and potential national security lapses.
Sen. Tim Scott, the outgoing Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced that Huang will testify publicly before the panel on Dec. 3. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the incoming chair, said the Trump administration needs to explain what role U.S. officials played in what she called a "reckless" decision.
Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's direct involvement with Nvidia's decision-making "raises serious national security and corruption questions."
"We must investigate these actions," said Garcia of California.
Nvidia was already facing sharp scrutiny from Congress after Huang acknowledged a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials believed to be a spy. Putting Huang back in charge, after Trump said the board did "what we wanted them to do," raised stark concerns over the administration's role in the company that is central to the AI economy.
As Democrats prepare to take charge of Congress in January, they are mounting investigations into the Trump administration, particularly Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has close ties with the company. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month said he was frustrated by the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed, the company whose CEO, Alice Huang, was involved with Jensen Huang.
"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," said Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee.
"Congress has much to investigate," he said.
Huang is expected to appear for two days of interviews with three House committees next week, along with his public hearing at the Senate panel.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," said a joint statement from Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on China; Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., chairman of the House Intelligence Committee; and Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
"We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary's AI capabilities."
Of concern to Congress is whether Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, has been selling its chips to China, in violation of export controls as the U.S. tries to protect certain technology that is at the core of the AI race.
Earlier this year, members of Congress urged the U.S. Commerce Department to "suspend or reconsider" Nvidia's export licenses to China and to conduct a full national security review, according to a release earlier this month from Warren and a key Republican on the Senate banking committee, Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana.
"Since then, NVIDIA has reportedly received approvals to export hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China's military, all while attempting to influence the debate over chip controls in Washington, D.C.," they wrote in a statement in November.
"NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's confirmation of a relationship with a suspected spy for China's intelligence service makes these national security concerns even more urgent and raises important questions NVIDIA must answer," the two senators said.
While Republican leaders were mostly quiet on Huang's return to Nvidia, other Republicans spoke more forcefully Monday.
Texas Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his seat after Trump endorsed his GOP primary opponent, questioned the company's comment that the U.S. said there was no security risk.
"No national security risk? Based on what?" Cornyn posted. Cornyn asked whether the FBI did a defensive briefing of Huang to conclude there was no risk, "If not, why not?"
Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon wrote on social media that the U.S. cannot say it wants to win the AI competition and then give China its best technology. "Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China," wrote Bacon, who is retiring from Congress.
Ahead of the announcement but after Trump's call for Huang to be reinstated, Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga of Michigan, who lost reelection to a Democrat, posted: "Ummm… she was, and is, a spy. How about we get serious about making sure China doesn't steal US company technology?"
Utah Sen. John Curtis asked similar questions.
"Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board?" Curtis asked. "And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?"
Democrats are preparing to dive more deeply into questions of national security and political corruption in Washington as they take over the committee gavels in January.
"The guy who was having an affair with a Chinese spy while working relentlessly to help China get access to as many AI chips as possible? Really?" posted Delaware Sen. Chris Coons, who is poised to become the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee when Democrats take the majority.
Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, said that Congress should investigate "what stock positions took place before the announcement."
Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who will chair the Senate finance committee and serves on the Senate intelligence committee, said Huang's restatement shows that under Trump and his administration, "our national security is for sale."
"In January, Democrats will hold this corrupt administration accountable," Wyden said.
Associated Press writers Kevin Freking, Aamer Madhani, Joey Cappelletti and Chris Rugaber contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.
Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.
The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.
Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.
In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.
However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.
Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.
Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

articles.title_orig: NATO warns Putin could strike before European army responds, points to US as military model
articles.title_zh: NATO warns Putin could strike before European army responds, points to US as military model
articles.content_orig:
Polish airspace violations by suspected Russian missiles trigger a stern warning from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, as Jon Scott reports. Rutte declares that the alliance will defend every inch of Polish territory. This escalation coincides with a devastating Russian missile strike on a residential apartment building in Kyiv, where rescuers search the ruins.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned Monday that creating a separate European army could undermine the alliance’s ability to respond quickly to a Russian attack, as Moscow continues to ramp up its military capabilities during the ongoing war in Ukraine.
Speaking at the 72nd annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin , Rutte cautioned that competing military command structures could hold up decisions in a crisis, warning that Russia’s "war machine" is running at full throttle and could also pose a threat to Europe long after the war ends.
"What I would counsel against is having all the nations with their own militaries working together in NATO and then on top of that having a big European structure, because then if Putin attacks, we will first need two or three weeks to agree who will do what, and then he will probably end up in Rotterdam before we have decided. So that has been my argument," Rutte said, according to Ukrainska Pravda .
NATO JETS SHOOT DOWN DRONE IN LITHUANIAN AIRSPACE AS RUSSIA GROWS 'INCREASINGLY RECKLESS,' RUTTE SAYS
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks to the media during a joint news conference with the members of the Bosnian Presidency in Sarajevo, Bosnia, Monday, March 10, 2025. (Armin Durgut)
Rutte pointed to the United States as a model for an integrated military, arguing that European countries would also need to move beyond separate national forces to establish a unified army.
"My point has always been that if you have a European military, you cannot also have national militaries. The United States has one military."
"There is not a specific army or navy for the state of New York or for the state of California. It is an integrated United States military. If Europe is able to pull that off, fine," Rutte said.
Rutte said it was Russia's expanding military production and cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea that pose a long-term threat to NATO, regardless of how the war in Ukraine ends.
"We face great dangers coming from Russia and the fact that Russia works so closely together with Iran, China, and North Korea, we know that Russia's war machine at the moment is running at full speed," Rutte also said at the assembly in Berlin.
FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE
Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery following what authorities said was a Ukrainian drone strike during the Russia-Ukraine conflict in Moscow, Russia, on Sept. 20, 2026. (REUTERS/Stringer)
"Its war economy keeps growing, and it won't stand still when the war against Ukraine hopefully will end one day. That whole machine is there and will continue."
Rutte also rejected the idea that only countries bordering Russia or Ukraine face a direct military threat, warning that Moscow's long-range missiles put capitals across Europe within striking distance.
"Let me say once again to everyone here who is not on the eastern flank: I have news for you. You are on the eastern flank too. These latest Russian missiles need only five minutes longer to reach Lisbon, Rome or The Hague, my hometown, than to reach Tallinn, Warsaw or Helsinki," Rutte said.
"So we are all on the eastern flank here. Let's put an end to this discussion about whether or not you are on the eastern flank. We are all on the eastern flank."
The NATO chief's remarks came amid plans to deploy an early-warning aircraft to Poland after Polish prosecutors said three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles landed on Polish territory Friday during strikes against Ukraine.
NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK
Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski during an inteview with Fox News Digital in Warsaw, Poland. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said that NATO would deploy an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to strengthen surveillance along the alliance's eastern flank, according to Reuters .
"This is a very good system that gives us even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat," Zalewski told reporters following a NATO meeting in Brussels.
The aircraft can monitor large areas of airspace and provide allied forces with a shared picture of potential aerial threats, improving NATO's ability to detect and respond to missile and aircraft activity.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also warned Monday night that intelligence indicated Moscow was preparing a new wave of strikes against Ukraine.
Beyond Russia's ongoing military threats, Rutte said that Europe's interconnected infrastructure, including energy networks and communications systems, is vulnerable.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT
Smoke rises in the city during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine August 31, 2026. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)
"We are all targeted, that we are all affected when it comes to our pipelines, our cables, our energy grids, and our economies."
"They are all interconnected, and that means that we are all in this for the long term. And therefore, we must step up to the plate to ensure that we stay ahead of danger."
Rutte said defending NATO countries demands civilian preparedness, pointing to northern European nations that have begun teaching residents about their responsibilities in the event of war.
"This really takes the whole of society," he said.
"And that's in the end, I think, still Norway and Sweden, and Denmark and Finland, and maybe one or two others who are really ahead of the pack here, and having made clear to their citizens what they need to do in case war breaks out, at least not to get in the way of the military, but to be helpful and also how they make sure that the police and the ambulance services and fire, the fire fighting departments work together, supporting the military wherever possible."
Rutte's warnings come amid uncertainty over Ukraine's long-term security arrangements and whether Western allies will offer guarantees resembling NATO's Article 5 collective defense commitment as part of a future peace agreement.

articles.title_orig: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.title_zh: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.content_orig:
The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill .
“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.
In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
“No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X .
President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.”
“One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”
Lawmakers made clear they still need answers.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3.
“The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement.
A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1.
“There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.”
“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida.
The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed , the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang , the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved.
Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.”
But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.”
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.”
“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”
“Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said.
Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said .
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny.
“Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media.
“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”
“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”

The Federal Reserve’s Inspector General is examining whether Michelle Bowman broke the Fed’s quiet-period rules at a private Bank of America dinner, according to a Bloomberg News report.
Bloomberg, citing one person familiar with the matter, reported that the inspector general’s office had asked to speak with Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, in recent weeks. Seeking Alpha wrote that it wasn’t known whether a meeting happened, and it didn’t independently confirm the report.
The dinner took place in New York in June, hours after a Fed policy meeting. Fed officials may not comment publicly on monetary policy or the economy until the Friday after meetings that end Wednesday.
The invitation-only event drew executives from hedge funds and other Wall Street firms, the outlet wrote.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, sent the inspector general a letter in July. Bowman, a former Kansas banking commissioner appointed to the Fed by President Donald Trump in 2018, told the Journal she didn’t discuss monetary policy at the dinner and “has consistently complied with all applicable FOMC and ethics rules.”
The Federal Reserve's inner workings and independence from politics have come increasingly into question, particularly after Trump put massive pressure on former chair Jerome Powell to lower interest rates and tried to spin up a politically charged investigation into Fed spending on an office renovation.

NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. Nvidia’s board’s explanation for rehiring Huang should alarm everyone who cares about oversight.
Jensen Huang is CEO of Nvidia again. Eleven days after he resigned over a scandal involving an alleged affair — which China has called “ a smear ” — Nvidia’s board voted unanimously Monday to reinstate him. The scandal centered on a U.S. intelligence assertion that the woman was working for Beijing.
Wall Street cheered and the board may consider the scandal closed. It isn’t, though. As a former senior adviser on the House Oversight Committee, allow me to point out that among the things we still don’t know is who inside the Trump administration kept a suspected chip smuggler off the export blacklist — or why they did. Congress already has a list of people it intends to question about this matter, but the list of current witnesses isn’t long enough to answer all the things Congress should want to know.

In August 2025, Commerce Department investigators were reportedly months into a probe of Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company suspected of diverting Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China. That’s when, according to The New York Times and Bloomberg , Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, contacted those investigators and told them he had permission from Jeffrey Kessler, the undersecretary who oversees export controls and reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, to reach out. The investigators were alarmed. The Justice Department took over the case and the Commerce Department stood down. MS NOW has not confirmed this reporting.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC that the Treasury, the Pentagon, the trade representative and the State Department had all wanted Megaspeed blacklisted, “but Commerce has the pen.” The pen belongs to Lutnick. While the Commerce Department has defended its actions and claimed along with the DOJ to have “ an extremely strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice,” Lutnick’s department has gone more than a year without adding a single company to its export blacklist. For some context, from 2018 to 2024, the Bureau of Industry and Security issued Entity List additions roughly every 35 days on average. Last week, the Commerce Department moved to close a loophole that let Chinese companies rent Nvidia’s computing power from other countries. But instead of giving anyone comfort, the move raised the question of why it took Huang’s scandal for the Commerce Department to act.
President Donald Trump defended Huang and Lutnick from the start. He says national security was never at risk, that he has no plans to replace Lutnick and that he is not sure Huang’s paramour was a spy. The New York Times reports that Trump called Huang two days before he resigned to urge him to fight for his job. On Sunday night, the president posted on social media that he hoped Nvidia’s board would rehire Huang, and by Monday morning, it had.
The board’s explanation for rehiring Huang should alarm everyone who cares about oversight. Directors say they received input from “senior levels of the United States government” and, on that basis, are confident Huang’s return poses no risk to national security. They did not say who assured them or what evidence supported that assurance. If that reported input came from the Commerce Department, then the agency accused of shielding Nvidia’s customer has now vouched for Nvidia’s chief executive. In a Monday morning interview with CNBC, Trump acknowledged that he provided input to the board .
Thus, it falls on Congress to investigate. There are many questions lawmakers should ask, including whether it was Lutnick who ignored the objections of four other agencies and decided against blacklisting Megaspeed. Is Nvidia’s lawyer’s report about getting permission from Kessler, the commerce undersecretary, true? If so, what exactly was he given permission to do, and did Lutnick know about it? Given the reports that intelligence officials briefed the president about a year ago, why was Huang never given a defensive briefing, and why did the administration keep approving Nvidia’s chip sales to China? What did Trump and Huang discuss on the phone before he resigned?
Trump tells CNBC he spoke to Nvidia board directly about Jensen Huang
What is the damage assessment? If Huang was the target of an intelligence operation, we should assume every communication he made during the relationship may have been monitored and every device he left unattended may have been opened. How much more is there? Almost none of the underlying records — the emails, the texts, the travel logs and the intelligence assessments — have reached the public yet.
Based on the current witness list, however, the investigation won’t be thorough enough to answer those questions. Lutnick has agreed to appear voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., on Dec. 10. Huang, after blowing a deadline and being threatened with a subpoena, has agreed to a closed-door , transcribed interview with three House committees on Dec. 1. Teter will follow on Dec. 2. Scott’s office says Huang will also testify in public before the Senate Banking Committee, but no date has been set. Kessler has not publicly responded to his invitation to a Dec. 3 House hearing.
Closed-door interviews are not accountability, and at this point, Huang won’t appear as a disgraced former executive but as the chief executive of the most important chip company on earth.
You’ll notice that the only fully public testimony scheduled will feature Lutnick, who gets to testify to a friendly chair a month before the gavel changes hands. Huang is scheduled to appear behind closed doors, but closed-door interviews are not accountability, and at this point, Huang won’t appear as a disgraced former executive but as the chief executive of the most important chip company on earth, with the president’s blessing and a board that has already declared itself satisfied.
When Democrats take the gavels in January, they should hold public hearings, subpoena every communication between Nvidia and the Commerce Department about Megaspeed and put Huang, Teter, Kessler and Lutnick under oath. However, because I spent years advising the House Oversight Committee, I know that in an effective investigation, you do not start with the chief executive of a company or a Cabinet secretary. You start with the junior staffers, the career export-control officers who cannot afford to pay outside counsel $1,200 an hour. You first ask the junior staffers who gave them the order to stand down. Then you work upstream.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., have already told Lutnick, the State Department and the White House to preserve their records on Nvidia’s China sales. Everyone who touched the Megaspeed matter should assume that every email, every text and every calendar entry will become public.
Anyone who has been through a congressional investigation knows that what is public is a fraction of what exists. We have not yet seen a single email, text message or interview transcript. The Justice Department has an open criminal inquiry into Megaspeed. There is an avalanche of information that has not entered the public domain, and it’s likely that all of it will eventually. The board has bet the company that whatever comes out next will not make things worse, and the directors now own every revelation that follows. (Erin Hooley | AP) An ad for the prediction market app Kalshi is displayed on a mobile phone Thursday, April 16, 2026, in Chicago.
Kalshi, the prediction market that has been in a legal battle with Utah’s government for much of 2026, has decided to “pause operations” in the state, it told The Salt Lake Tribune on Monday afternoon.
Users who now try to use Kalshi here see a message telling them that “some markets are unavailable in Utah.”
Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said the company “made the difficult decision” to suspend operations after a federal court ruled that Utah could enforce its gambling laws, and while Kalshi awaits a decision on another case being pursued by the federal government’s Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which is seeking to allow Kalshi to operate unfettered in the state.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick said. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”
After Monday’s pause in operations, Utahns who had accounts on Kalshi can no longer open new contracts on the site, but can exit currently held positions and withdraw funds, McGavick said.
In August, Judge Robert J. Shelby ruled against Kalshi in the company’s lawsuit against Utah in federal court, saying the state could pursue enforcement of its anti-gambling laws against Kalshi’s so-called event contracts, which allow users to place bets on the outcomes of political races, sports, the weather and other future events.
But the court has not yet ruled in the CFTC’s lawsuit against Utah, which sought to stop the state from taking action against Kalshi and other prediction markets offering event contracts. That suit argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction to regulate prediction markets, bypassing state laws. Crypto.com’s exchange also filed suit against Utah in November, and the cases have been consolidated by Shelby.
On Friday, Shelby held a hearing in the CFTC case. While he did not issue a formal ruling, he did say companies like Kalshi are subject to state gambling laws and that the federal government may have “a steep hill to climb” to convince him otherwise, FOX 13 reported .
Kalshi co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, meanwhile, face 14 criminal charges — including 13 felony counts — after Utah Attorney General Derek Brown accused them of breaking the state’s gambling laws.
Last Wednesday, the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in a 2-1 decision that Maryland could enforce its sports-wagering law against Kalshi. Utah was one of 36 states that joined to file an amicus brief supporting Maryland in the suit. The 6th and 9th Circuits have also ruled against Kalshi, while the 3rd Circuit ruled in its favor, likely setting up a Supreme Court case to decide the issue moving forward.

Key Nvidia partners and suppliers in Asia saw their shares skyrocket on Tuesday as investors piled back into the tech market, following the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang by its board.
Taiwan's TSMC, a critical partner to the U.S. chip giant, surged almost 10%, with Hon Hai Precision Industry — known also as Foxconn — also up by the same amount. Nvidia partner Mediatek also spiked 10%.
Taipei's stock exchange has a daily price limit of 10% for stocks.
In South Korea, Nvidia suppliers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix jumped 8% and 10% respectively.The two companies, which together make up over 40% of the Kospi's weighting, sent the index up over 7%. South Korea's LG Electronics soared 16.02%.
The rise in the index triggered the Korea Exchange's sidecar on the index, reportedly making it the 100th sidecar the KRX has activated.
Japan's Softbank Group Corp , a major investor in the chip space, climbed over 8%. Semiconductor test company Advantest , as well as counterpart Tokyo Electron , jumped 15% and 12% each. Both companies are collaborators with Nvidia.
"Jensen's return is particularly welcome for Asian technology stocks, many of which suffered collateral damage from Nvidia's leadership crisis," Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist at Saxo said in a note Tuesday morning.
However, she points out that the recovery will likely favor established companies with visible orders, strong balance sheets and pricing power, compared to those who rely on "years of uninterrupted AI spending."
Nvidia's stock had closed up 31% following Huang's reinstatement. It had previously shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8.

articles.content_orig:
Topic: State and Territory Elections
Labor is set for a potentially catastrophic result in the Victorian state election and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will want to give it a wide berth. ( AAP Image: Jay Kogler )
One unexpected benefit of Anthony Albanese's summit season, beyond pushing Australia's agenda on the world stage, is that the prime minister could avoid Victoria.
Labor faces a potentially catastrophic result in the state election this weekend, and the federal wing will want to give it a wide berth. Insiders say they expect a result as bad as what hit NSW Labor in 2011, after its litany of scandals.
A wholesale rejection of the NSW Labor brand in 2011 over sleaze and corruption led to the loss of 30 seats. The primary vote plummeted to 25.6 per cent.
The NSW Labor brand became a pariah and shorthand for shonky behaviour and dodgy deals. Those outside the state would go to great lengths to distance themselves from that version of the Labor Party.
The Bracks/Brumby government was by no means without flaw, but in Victoria the criticisms were largely confined to policy issues, not character and systemic behaviour.
Now, that cloud of alleged corruption is being investigated by a royal commission. Claims of wrongdoing within the CFMEU over key government infrastructure projects look set to be the one reason Victorians turn their back on state Labor.
The polls put the Liberals on track for a majority, and Labor could be reduced to a rump of as few as 20 seats or even less in the Legislative Assembly.
We may see a blue-nami sweep across Victoria on Saturday, but there is still a chance One Nation could win a handful of seats and hold balance of power in the upper house. That would be pretty impressive for Victoria.
One insider said they would be relieved to end up with 35 seats, losing only 21. But many I spoke with expect Labor to lose 30 to 35 seats.
It is possible Labor could lose up to 35 seats, including that of Premier Ben Carroll. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica )
Many long-time Labor voters cannot bring themselves to vote for a Labor government now associated with three things: crime, debt and corruption.
The CFMEU corruption allegations and the perception that billions have been wasted have deprived Labor of the ability to talk about its record of infrastructure delivery. The term "Big Build" is now a negative — voters think of waste, mismanagement and corruption.
The writing has been on the wall for a while: the Werribee by-election in early 2025 saw a 16.5 percentage point swing against Labor on first preferences. And that was before the recent surge of support for One Nation.
The Liberals have sought to make this a referendum on a 12-year-old government and its record of mistakes and failures.
Ben Carroll has tried to set a new direction and signal to voters that this is a new government. But the Liberals have managed to tie him back to Andrews and Allan and a long list of gripes — out-of-control crime, net debt forecast to reach almost $200 billion by 2029-30, and CFMEU allegations.
It is telling that Dan Andrews still features in Liberal ads when he has not been premier for more than three years.
Most in federal Labor believe that since COVID, Andrews and his colleagues have been a drag on their vote. They would never admit it publicly, but there is a view that if Victorians take out their frustration on Labor this Saturday, it offers more than a reset.
If Kew MP and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson becomes premier, the honeymoon will be short. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica )
And if the Liberals' Jess Wilson becomes premier, she should not expect a long honeymoon. The sentiment among many Victorians is simple and blunt — not Labor.
If the polls are right and the Liberals win, it will be off the back of voters who have switched allegiances, plus others fed up with both major parties and who back One Nation's populist broken-system mantra.
These voters are unlikely to give Wilson an easy run; they will judge her on how quickly she can get on and fix the long list of things she has called Labor out on.
From potholes to budget black holes, she will have a long and tricky to-do list. She should brace for being judged on making good on her commitments to improve services and fix crime and will also need to appoint a capable cabinet that she needs to serve as a competent government.
The final week of the state election campaign comes alongside the last week of the parliamentary year. The last week of the parliamentary year is often known as the killing season, but there will be no political carnage at the national level this week — only a desperation for Federal Labor to ignore whatever is going on down south and capitalise on a frenzy to get bills passed to establish an image of a government in feverish activity.

The update came during a November 16 briefing to the Brazos Valley Intergovernmental Committee, according to local broadcaster KBTX. Institute director Steve Putna said practical training would prepare students to enter Terafab’s workforce.

That distinction matters: this is an update on a university training and research facility, not an announcement that Tesla or SpaceX has received a new university funding package.
KBTX reports that the institute building is about 20% complete. Leaders expect substantial building completion around the end of 2027, followed by equipment installation and significant operations in mid-2028.

It describes the RELLIS Campus facility as a shared-use center for semiconductor research and domestic fabrication. Its earlier schedule called for building occupancy in May 2028.
For Terafab, hiring and training are another part of a much larger build-out.
