Looking for a web browser without Google Chrome underneath? You can try this independent web browser now on macOS and Linux.
Looking for a web browser without Google Chrome underneath? You can try this independent web browser now on macOS and Linux.
Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling announced that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development.
The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We’ve seen many engines emerge over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. While Gecko, now used in Mozilla Firefox, first appeared in Netscape 6 in 2000 , Apple’s WebKit arrived in Safari in 2003 as a fork of KDE’s KHTML. A decade later, the Google-backed Chromium project forked WebKit to create Blink, which now powers Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera, and more.
Ladybird is backed by a nonprofit organization with the goal of creating “an independent, fast and secure browser that respects user privacy and fosters an open web,” according to its website . Though Ladybird development initially began as part of a C++ project, its developers eventually began porting the code to Rust using AI .
In his post announcing the alpha, Kling notes that the browser built around the Ladybird engine “is modest but functional,” adding that “some websites won’t work” during the alpha. A Windows version of Ladybird will arrive during a “later stage” of the project.

articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — By his own account, President Donald Trump was watching the stock market slide and decided to stop it. He would take it upon himself to determine who should lead one of the nation’s largest companies. Never mind national security concerns, never mind the autonomy of the private sector. Trump would decide.
The president’s extraordinary intervention resulted in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced out amid a Chinese espionage scandal. Trump then got the result he sought. Sagging stock markets shot back up, restoring nearly $1 trillion in value alone to investors of Nvidia, who happen to include himself.
Everything about Trump’s handling of the scandal behind Huang’s fall and swift rise again has been astonishing: The president’s denial that he knew about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset even though reports indicate he was informed at least twice. His shoulder-shrugging nonchalance about one of his tech lord donors in bed with an asset for a hostile power. And now his decision to bolster the wealth of investors over the warnings of his own intelligence agencies.
“I’m doing it for the country,” Trump told CNBC on Monday morning shortly after Nvidia’s board bowed to his wishes. He explained that he had seen the markets collectively lose trillions of dollars in recent days, driven in part by the Huang scandal. “I watched that and, you know, I better get involved. If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
The seeming trade of long-term national security concerns for a short-term stock rally sent shock waves through Washington, Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Even fellow Republicans, already unsettled by the Nvidia scandal, expressed consternation at the lack of accountability demonstrated by Huang’s quick return to the executive suite. Lawmakers in both parties cried foul and vowed to investigate.
“There is something profoundly wrong about Jensen Huang having a relationship with a Chinese Communist Spy and helping China get a huge number of very advanced computer chips when that was specifically against the policy of the United States Government and now he is being reinstated as ceo of the most advanced chip making company in the world,” former Speaker Newt Gingrich, a strong Trump ally, wrote online.
Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., a member of the Senate Banking Committee that is scheduled to hear testimony from Huang on Dec. 3, said Congress should examine Trump’s communications with both Huang and the Nvidia board to determine what he assured or promised them.
“The administration’s top priority should be safeguarding our national security and ensuring America’s most powerful technologies serve the American people, not our adversaries,” Reed said in a statement. The economy, he added, depends on rule of law and fair dealing. “President Trump’s improper interventions damage these principles and must be investigated.”
As if Trump’s actions were not unusual enough, his public celebration of his successful arm-twisting only exacerbated the furor. Shortly after Nvidia restored Huang, Trump posted a bizarre image on social media portraying the once-and-future corporate CEO as a martyr.
The image appeared to be an AI composite based on the famous photo of Trump after he survived an attempted assassination at a 2024 rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, surrounded by Secret Service agents, blood on his face, pumping his fist in the air. In the version that the president shared online, Huang was at the center of the frame, with blood on his face, holding up a red bra. Behind him waved a flag that said “Nvidia.”
The surreal post seemed to sum up Trump’s often flippant, from-the-gut, anything-goes approach to the presidency, in which his whims become official policy. With the image, he managed to mock both the seriousness of political violence and a major espionage operation all at once — flicking both off with a reference to women’s undergarments, as if it were a sexual conquest.
“You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks,” Trump told The New York Times on Monday morning.
As he has several times in recent days, Trump simply rejected the conclusions of his own U.S. intelligence agencies that the businesswoman involved with Huang was conducting espionage for China.
“Every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy,” he told CNBC. But, he added, “with Jensen, I don’t believe that’s true.”
Whether Trump believes something is true matters more than contrary facts or investigations. His disregard of intelligence about Chinese interference in American affairs echoes his disregard of the intelligence about Russian interference in American affairs back in his first term. At CIA headquarters in Langley, few have forgotten Trump’s meeting in Helsinki with President Vladimir Putin of Russia in 2018, when the U.S. president took the word of his Russian counterpart over that of his own intelligence agencies about Moscow’s meddling in the U.S. election in 2016.
At other times, Trump has seemed to accept that, in fact, perhaps the businesswoman involved with Huang really was working for the Chinese. But even then, he expressed no particular distress about it. “We spy on China, they spy on us,” he told Fox News last week when he landed in Shenzhen, China, for meetings hosted by President Xi Jinping of China.
That, in turn, echoed his first-term equivalence when asked why he respected Putin, who was described as a killer. “We’ve got a lot of killers,” Trump said. “What, do you think our country’s so innocent?”
He continues to embrace Putin, with whom he met in Shenzhen. In another provocative social media message in recent days, Trump posted a photo of the two of them shaking hands under the caption “My Friend,” touching off a storm of protest in Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe.
The timing of the recent public disclosure of Huang’s involvement with the alleged Chinese asset proved uncomfortable for Trump, who was focused on his upcoming meeting with the Chinese leader. He made clear while in China that he had no intention of challenging Xi over the matter. While Trump said he did discuss the case “at length” in their private conversations, he characterized it not as a complaint about the espionage but a lament over the “tragedy” for Huang. China has denied the spying allegations, and the businesswoman has not commented.
Trump has been more aggressive about trying to steer the decisions of individual private companies than other presidents. He has pressured corporations to eliminate diversity programs, sought to force changes to pricing practices and asserted the power to advance mergers that he favored. Among other things, he pushed Huang’s Nvidia last year to give the federal government a share of revenue on certain semiconductor chips to China connected to export licensing policy, essentially making the government a partner in Nvidia’s business in China.
Nor is Trump himself a completely disinterested player to the drama playing out at the company. He owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock as of the end of last year, according to his financial disclosure report, and his brokerage accounts continued to buy and sell Nvidia shares as recently as September. Nvidia has also donated $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and at least $20 million for construction of his White House ballroom, one of the president’s biggest priorities.
It mattered, too, that Trump has become personally acquainted with Huang and considers him an ally. “On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen,” he wrote on social media, “and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure.”

The chipmaker's board reinstated Huang as CEO Monday, and President Trump says he " convinced " them. "I don't think anybody could revive the stock like it's being revived right now," Trump said.
The stock jumped about 31%, adding about $950 billion in market value, the biggest one-day gain ever. The old record, Microsoft's ( MSFT ) $450 billion jump in July, isn't even half of it. It also tops the record one-day loss, Nvidia's own $593 billion drop on DeepSeek day in January 2025.
The surge lifted Nvidia past Microsoft and Alphabet ( GOOGL ).
Top companies change places all the time, usually by a few billion dollars. Only one other company has jumped into the top two past a rival that much bigger. On Jan. 3, 2001, a surprise Fed rate cut sent Cisco from No. 6 to No. 2 in one day, past Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), which was worth nearly 30% more.
Cisco is on the other end of the ledger, too. Its $274 billion slide from No. 1 to No. 4 in 2000 was the biggest fall from the top until this month. It never got the crown back.
Nvidia did both in three weeks. It lost nearly $2 trillion in 13 trading days, falling from No. 1 on Nov. 3 to No. 4 on Friday, including nearly $900 billion last week alone, the worst week any company has ever had.
Wall Street spent last week dumping anything tied to AI. It spent a wild Monday buying it back . Nasdaq 100 futures hit their 7% overnight limit for the first time since it was widened in 2020, and the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) closed up nearly 7%.
The rest of the chip sector came along for the ride. A Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks added about $2 trillion in market value, and about half of that was Nvidia. Memory makers SK Hynix ( SKHY ) and Micron ( MU ) rose about 20%, adding roughly $270 billion between them. Intel ( INTC ) gained 16%, while AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) lagged with single-digit gains.
Not everyone is ready to move on. Bernstein upgraded the stock on Monday but called the board's on-again, off-again response " frankly, clown-like ."
Trump isn't sweating the details. "I run the country," he said. "I don't run Nvidia, but Nvidia is a big part of it."

A tech snafu at one of the world’s busiest airports on Sunday is delaying thousands of Delta Airlines flights headed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
An issue with Delta Airlines’ weight and balance system at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is responsible for the delay at one of the busiest airports in the country, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement posted on social media.
More than 3,550 flights traveling within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed as of Sunday afternoon, according to Flight Aware .
The governmental agency urged travelers to check in with the airline for the latest information on their flights, and said that steps have already been taken to fix the issue.
“Delta is working to resolve issues with the airline’s weight and balance automation system,” the FAA statement said. “These delays are not related to any FAA air traffic systems.”
Delta said it is working limit congestion at its Atlanta hub.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” said Delta spokesperson Natalie Duggan. “We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism."
The issue on Sunday comes after a communications failure grounded all flights nationwide earlier this month, leading New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to call for the removal of U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Other recent technological malfunctions have impacted other industries, including online banking systems and Microsoft Outlook.
Delta Airlines did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Gothamist.

Citi Bike members will soon pay less for electric bike rides under a new agreement between Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration and Lyft, which operates the bike-share program.
The deal will also freeze annual membership prices and other fees for members through May 2029.
Starting Jan. 19, 2027, Citi Bike members will pay no more than $3.65 for an e-bike ride lasting up to 45 minutes. The cap also applies to reduced-fare members and shorter rides that already cost less will remain at their current price.
Annual membership prices, member per-minute e-bike fees and charges for rides that exceed 45 minutes will be frozen at current rates until May 26, 2029, when Lyft’s contract with the city expires.
“Getting around New York City shouldn't come with a price tag that keeps climbing by the minute,” Mamdani wrote in a release announcing the agreement. “Because a more affordable city is one where getting around it doesn’t break the bank.”
Citi Bike members currently pay 27 cents per minute for e-bike rides, or $12.15 for a 45-minute ride, except for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, which are capped at $5.40. The annual membership fee is $239 and rides on regular bikes lasting up to 45 minutes are included.
Under the new agreement, members could save as much as $8.50 on a single e-bike ride, according to City Hall. The new cap replaces the existing $5.40 cap for rides entering or leaving Manhattan, as well as a one-time allotment of 60 e-bike minutes for members.
The agreement doesn't prohibit Lyft from increasing Citi Bike prices for non-members, who currently pay $4.99 for a ride up to 30 minutes on analog bikes and an additional 41 cents per-minute for e-bike rides.
The city has also agreed to help install electric charging infrastructure at more than 130 Citi Bike stations starting next year. This will allow the e-bikes to recharge while docked, rather than having Lyft workers swap out depleted batteries. City officials said the changes will reduce operating costs and make more e-bikes available to riders.
City Councilmember Lincoln Restler introduced a bill two years ago to rein in the rising cost of Citi Bike rides.
“ This is such a tremendous victory for Citi Bike riders,” Restler said. “The city had given Lyft a monopoly, essentially, with the Citi Bike program and the cost spiraled out of control in such a way where it felt like New Yorkers were being taken advantage of.”
Citi Bike raised prices six times from 2022 through January 2026, with Lyft recently blaming tariffs and inflation for the need to raise rates.
“We’re grateful to Mayor Mamdani and Commissioner Flynn for working with us to make Citi Bike an even more sustainable, reliable, and affordable option for New Yorkers,” Patrick Knoth, general manager of Citi Bike, wrote in a statement.

GTA 6 leaker Cyberleek has reportedly released the executable file for the leaked Xbox build of the game, prompting concern that an unofficial PC port could follow.
The leak comes via the same group that shared leaked footage and threatened to release additional videos unless Rockstar changed its all-digital launch strategy a week before Rockstar released its extended gameplay teaser on Netflix . The group then threatened to release a full build of the game, including its full story mode and end credits.
Now, as reported by IGN , Cyberleek has released the .exe for the incomplete Xbox build, with some predicting that AI-assisted recompilation of the build could get GTA 6 running on PC within days.
The file was released alongside a new statement in which Cyberleek claimed their actions were about "fighting anti-consumerism in the games industry."
They also referenced Take-Two's efforts to stop the leaks and identify whoever is behind them, saying: "Months of takedowns, subpoenas and wallet tracing later, the hunt is still on and the uploads keep arriving."
Cyberleek also pushed back on claims that the leaks are little more than a crypto scheme, insisting the crypto was used to raise money for a secret project unrelated to the game. "There is no other way to move funds without names," they said, "and this work requires no names."
According to IGN, the leaked Xbox build runs counter to the idea that Cyberleek only had access to an early build.
Take-Two previously issued subpoenas to companies including Discord as part of its search for those responsible for the leaks. It remains unclear how this build got out of Rockstar.

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

articles.title_orig: States sue Musk companies over flood of sexualized images made with AI chatbot Grok
articles.title_zh: States sue Musk companies over flood of sexualized images made with AI chatbot Grok
articles.content_orig:
Lawsuits against Elon Musk's SpaceX are stacking up, with Virginia and Oregon becoming the first states to sue the company over issues with its Grok AI image generator.
Versions of Grok and SpaceX's social network X have enabled users to generate and distribute explicit deepfakes based on real photos or videos of children and other people who did not consent, according to research by the Internet Watch Foundation , the Center for Countering Digital Hate and others.
In separate complaints submitted to state courts as of Monday morning, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones argued that SpaceX failed to put safeguards in place to stop Grok and X users from making and sharing harmful deepfake images, especially alleged AI-generated child sexual abuse material.
The complaints also allege that SpaceX has falsely represented its AI apps and social network (Grok and X) as generally safe, which the states see as a violation of Virginia's Consumer Protection Act or Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act. The matter is particularly concerning because X allows minors 13 and older to access its content.
Rayfield and Jones both noted in their complaints that harms caused by non-consensual, sexualized images go beyond the victims depicted in the images.
"This content can cause fear, distress, and anxiety in those who are unwillingly exposed to the content," Jones wrote. Rayfield wrote that such conduct "erodes important norms regarding consent and privacy and trivializes sexual imagery, abuse, and exploitation."
In a statement emailed to CNBC by a spokesperson for SpaceXSI, and posted on the company's @Safety account on X, the company said, "When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement. Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors."
At an NYC Council hearing in October , a SpaceX AI policy leader, Gabriela Castillo Madrid, said the company had appropriate "safeguards" and "strict controls" in place around its AI products.
SpaceX was already facing multiple Grok- and X-related lawsuits, and government probes around the world, including by authorities in the U.K., Spain, Ireland, France and the state of California.
In private-sector lawsuits filed against SpaceX in the U.S. concerning Grok and AI-generated, explicit images, litigation is still in early stages and is tracked by The Center for Internet Technology Addiction.
When the city of Baltimore sued xAI, now owned and operated by SpaceX, the company argued that under Section 230, they were not liable for unwanted images. Section 230 is a federal law that largely shields online platforms from liability for users' content.
SpaceX also sued a user in a federal court in the Northern District of Texas for breach of contract after he allegedly used Grok to create and distribute deepfake explicit images, including depictions of minors. Lawyers for Musk's company argued that Grok should be seen as "a neutral tool, subject to user control," and that any image generation "is the result of the user's prompts and directions."
The new state suits add to legal pressure on SpaceX. Both Virginia and Oregon are seeking injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, while Virginia is also seeking restitution for consumers from Musk's company.
Oregon submitted its complaint to the Multnomah County Circuit Court on Sunday evening, and Virginia submitted its complaint to the City of Richmond Circuit Court Monday morning . As of early Monday, the suits were pending the courts' acceptance.
State attorneys general have recently succeeded in compelling U.S. social media companies to change their products and pay for alleged past harms.
In August, for example, Meta settled a major federal case centered on allegations that the social media giant misrepresented the level of child mental health problems caused by its apps, Facebook and Instagram . Without admitting to wrongdoing, Meta agreed to pay states around $17 billion over a 10-year period and to make app changes that experts believe will help keep children safer online.

articles.title_orig: Fed's John Williams indicates higher interest rates likely 'over time' to address inflation
articles.title_zh: Fed's John Williams indicates higher interest rates likely 'over time' to address inflation
articles.content_orig:
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said Monday that policymakers have more work to do to bring inflation under control, though he indicated that further action can unfold over time as the economy continues to grow.
In remarks consistent with previous statements , the influential central banker expressed confidence that inflation will get closer to the Fed's 2% target in 2027 before hitting the goal the following year. He also said that while artificial intelligence is pressuring prices, there's "little evidence" it will be the source of more persistent inflation.
"But getting inflation back to 2% is 100% essential," he said in remarks at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York. "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done."
The comments come at a delicate moment for monetary policy, as the economy continues to grow and inflation stays well above the Fed's goal.
Fed officials have differed over how quickly to raise rates, with some advocating more aggressive action while others, including Williams, have emphasized a measured approach.
Williams ascribed the current inflation pressures to the conflict in Iran, demand for goods associated with the AI build-out and tariffs, the effects of which he said "have largely abated" as a source of pressure. Nevertheless, he expressed confidence that inflation will subside substantially in 2027 even as economic growth remains robust and unemployment edges lower.
The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Dec. 8-9, with markets fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate increase from the current target range of 3.75%-4%. The remarks from Williams are expected to be the last major policy statement from any Fed official before the December decision.
"Monetary policy cannot move ships or reopen pipelines and refineries, but it can — and must — ensure that these shocks do not lead to broader or persistent inflationary dynamics or erode well-anchored inflation expectations," Williams said, according to his prepared remarks.
Williams did not explicitly address the December meeting expectations, instead pointing to the statement released after the prior FOMC meeting in late October that said the "accumulation of more information" will help decide the future policy path.
"The data that we have received since then show that the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high," he said.

articles.title_orig: Failure of Cop31 prompts calls for urgent reform of UN climate summits
articles.title_zh: Failure of Cop31 prompts calls for urgent reform of UN climate summits
articles.content_orig:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.
The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions .
Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.
Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.
Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been formal acknowledgment that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say, says Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations.
Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
"The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable," Bowen told the press after the agreement failed. "It's happening at speed and it's irreversible."
The disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels in climate conferences have a long, fractured history.
The COP process works by consensus, so nearly 200 countries must agree to a final text at the end of the negotiations. Some fossil fuel producers like Norway and Mexico have recently wanted to include transitioning away from fossil fuels in the text. Other large oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked adding fossil fuels to the final agreement.
At the climate talks in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time in 28 years of conferences to mention transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final agreement.
Deeply frustrated with this U.N. process, more than 50 countries have created their own separate conference dedicated to phasing out fossil fuels. In April, they held the "First International Conference for the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels" in Colombia. In 2027, Ireland and the Pacific Island nation of Tuvalu will co-host the second conference.
These side efforts are the best hope for climate action until something changes in the COP process, says Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama.
"I am an optimist by nature," he tells NPR, "but I am not an idiot."
This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.
Since the war began, countries across Asia and Africa have accelerated their transitions to solar energy, batteries and electric vehicles, and reduced their reliance on fossil fuels like oil and natural gas .
COP31 organizers promised that this would be the "electrification COP." Climate technologies like renewable energy, super-efficient heat pumps and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Many of these technologies are being manufactured in China, the main exporter of climate solutions.
The conference's initial goal was to increase global electrification from its current level of around 23% to 35% by 2035. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra," Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember, told NPR when COP31 began.
The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was signed on to by dozens of countries. However, that pledge did not ultimately pass, says Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate change think tank E3G. "Electrification was collateral damage when the whole decision cratered," he said.
The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. President Trump announced he would withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on his first day back in office in 2025. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.
An informal delegation of congressional Democrats did come to Turkey. They told delegates at COP31 that when Democrats control both chambers of Congress next year, climate change will return to the main agenda.
While the debate over fossil fuels stole the spotlight at this year's COP, a major focus of the negotiations has been on money. Countries debated new goals for funding to assist nations hardest hit by climate change.
Over the years at climate summits, lower-income countries have made the case that while they're responsible for only a small share of the emissions causing climate change, they're experiencing some of the worst disasters.
"We're not a nation that has the luxury of debating whether climate change is real for us," says Matthew Samuda, Jamaica's minister of water, environment and climate change. "The reality is, over the last five years, we have had a category 4 hurricane, a tropical storm and a category 5 hurricane. So climate change for us is indeed real and we are experiencing economic losses from a problem that we didn't create."
In 2024, nations agreed to eventually provide $1.3 trillion per year to developing nations, what's known as climate finance. Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024 , according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The majority of that goes to projects that reduce emissions, including renewable energy like solar and wind.
As climate disasters become costlier, lower-income countries have been pushing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts, such as protecting coastal communities from sea level rise and strengthening infrastructure against storms. The United Nations estimates that those nations' needs will reach $305 billion annually by 2035 .
The COP31 U.N. Climate Summit ended Sunday in Antalya, Turkey and tens of thousands of people attended what has become the longest summit in the history of these gatherings. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption

articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Gets Hero’s Welcome Upon Return To Nvidia HQ, Video Shows
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Gets Hero’s Welcome Upon Return To Nvidia HQ, Video Shows
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia on Monday announced Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO , effective immediately, a dramatic twist in a scandal that hammered the chipmaker's stock price and rocked the tech and artificial intelligence industries.
The board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him. The board added that it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and that it is confident Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk."
President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he had been speaking to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly," and that Huang "did nothing wrong." Trump said he talked to Huang on Sunday and asked him to promise to "work hard."
Huang resigned from his role as chief executive earlier this month after a series of shocking reports about multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The New York Times reported on Sunday that the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security during at least part of the time that she was engaging in a relationship with Huang.
Shares of Nvidia surged 33% following Huang's reinstatement. The stock had shed nearly 33% from the time Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on Nov. 8. The stock closed at $186.64 on Nov.6.
"I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process."
Senior government officials briefed Nvidia's board late last week and communicated that no national security laws were violated, according to sources familiar with the discussion who asked to remain anonymous because they were not authorized to speak publicly. That update prompted the board to reach out to Huang, the people said.
Huang and the board held their first conversations since his ouster on Saturday, and the group determined he would return as CEO during a second meeting on Sunday, the people said. Nvidia's cratering stock price played a role in accelerating those conversations.
Trump celebrated Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday, writing in a post on his social media site that the board made "the correct and proper decision" to reinstate him. Trump said the U.S. needs Huang's leadership to "ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy."
He reiterated that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
"On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure," Trump wrote.
Several tech industry leaders, including Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX , Gavin Baker, managing partner and chief investment officer at Atreides Management, and Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO, had been actively lobbying for Huang's return. Musk wrote in a post on X on Monday that the board's "mistake has been corrected."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
For weeks following Huang's ouster, the company's board maintained that it was not considering Huang's reinstatement. It appointed Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, as the chipmaker's interim CEO, who reiterated that position in an interview with CNBC following Huang's exit. Kress will continue to serve as Nvidia's CFO, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Nvidia's board formed an independent committee and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into Huang and whether company secrets or national security were compromised. The board said Monday that "the committee's investigation will proceed to conclusion" and that Huang is "committed to cooperating with it."
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia's board chair, Harvey Jones, said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company."
Even with Huang back at the helm, Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny over its chip sales in Southeast Asia and China.
Lawmakers have been preparing for investigations into how Huang's affair with the alleged spy may have damaged U.S. AI dominance, influenced his positions on export controls, and impacted his close relationships with Trump and his Cabinet. Huang has been one of the loudest voices opposing strict export controls on advanced chips.
"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., said in a statement Monday.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, is scheduled to appear before the panels on Dec. 2. Those dates were set before Huang's return, and John Fisher, who represents Huang, did not comment on whether there are any changes in his plans to testify.
Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Monday that Huang will publicly testify on Dec. 3 as the sole witness during a hearing titled, "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls."
"Americans deserve answers about what NVIDIA and the Trump administration knew, when they knew it, and whether sufficient steps were taken to prevent sensitive technology from falling into the wrong hands," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., a member of the Banking Committee, wrote in a post on X on Monday.

articles.title_zh: New York judge urged Kalshi to compromise on limiting bets by anyone under 21
articles.content_orig:
The move came after the New York AG sought a TRO against the prediction market.
The Trump administration tried unsuccessfully to step in after an attorney for the prediction market Kalshi warned Friday that the platform could be crippled if a judge grants a temporary restraining order being sought by New York state's attorney general.
New York Attorney General Letitia James requested the restraining order after U.S. District Judge Vernon Broderick on Friday denied Kalshi's attempt to move James' lawsuit against the platform from New York state court into federal court, ruling that prediction markets do not necessarily fall outside state jurisdiction.
After James asked New York Judge Melissa Crane to issue the restraining order to stop Kalshi from offering sports contracts without a license from the New York State Gaming Commission, Kalshi attorney Sean Murphy told Crane that "The TRO would likely force the liquidation of all open positions, disrupting markets far beyond this State."
Judge Crane set a hearing on the matter for Monday.
In an emergency telephone hearing Friday, the Trump administration urged another federal judge, Lorna Schofield, to prevent Crane from ruling on the TRO request.
"The temporary restraining order New York seeks would completely shut down Kalshi's operations nationwide," said Andrew Weisberg, an attorney for Kalshi's regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. "There is no greater irreparable harm than one of our regulated markets being completely disrupted."
An attorney for the New York attorney general's office, Kate Rhodes Janofsky, countered that there is no basis for the federal judge to intervene when there is a hearing in state court scheduled for Monday.
"They have to put in evidence of irreparable harm. They have not done so. There has been no evidence of market disruption," Janofsky said.
Judge Schofield agreed and declined to get involved. "The requested application is denied," she said.
James sued Kalshi in July , claiming that the platform violates New York state laws prohibiting wagering on games involving New York college teams and all sports betting for those under 21.
The lawsuit does not seek to shut Kalshi down -- but, if successful, it could force the prediction market to change the way it operates.

articles.content_orig:
Thousands of adult bed rails from China that were sold in the US have been recalled after an 89-year-old woman died of suffocation when she was trapped between the product and her mattress.
About 2,114 adult bed rails sold on Amazon by Guangzhou Yupin Technology Co. – a Chinese company doing business as Xentrawave – are included in the recall, according to the US Consumer Product Safety Commission.
All batches of Xentrawave’s model XT016 and batch number 20251212 of model XT026 are included in the recall for failing to meet mandatory safety requirements, because customers can be pinned between the rail and the side of the mattress – posing a risk of death by asphyxiation.
The XT106 model adult bed rail also doesn’t meet structural stability requirements and its push pins and push pin holes are incorrectly sized, posing a risk of laceration, the agency said.
The CPSC said it has received one report of a death related to the Xentrawave recall, involving the 89-year-old woman who died from asphyxiation.
Customers can find the model numbers XT016 or XT026 on the front of the product’s outer packaging and the first page of the instruction manual.
For the XT026 model, consumers can locate the batch number on the product label attached to the back of the bed rail’s gray fabric pouch and in the instruction manual.
Consumers should immediately stop use of the recalled bed rails and contact Xentrawave for a full refund.

They will be asked to cut the foam padding on the bed rail handles, disassemble the product and email a photo of the destroyed bed rail to xentrawavedirect@163.com or submit it online at https://xentrawahelp.com/xentrawave-bed-rail-safety-recall/ .
The recalled XT016 bed rails were sold on Amazon from May 2025 through March 2026 and the XT026 model was sold from March 2026 through August 2026. The bed rails cost between $37 and $40.

articles.content_orig:
Update [ Mon 23rd Nov 2026, 2:50pm ]: Well, the patch notes are out! Rockstar Games mentions seven official fixes for the update, and none of them are specifically to do with the Xbox Series S or other things like how bright the game is.
Nevertheless, there's always a chance they've made some extra tweaks under the hood.
Here are the official seven fixes in GTA 6's first post-launch update (November 23):
Original Story: GTA 6 only officially launched late last week, but Rockstar Games has already pushed out a new update (01.002.002) for the game across Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S (along with PS5), rolling out as of a few hours ago.
You're looking at a download size of around 1.6GB for update 1.0.2 on Xbox Series X and S.
In terms of what's included, Rockstar has yet to issue any official patch notes, and we'll have to wait and see whether anything is distributed. We'll obviously update this article with the patch notes if they're made available to us.
Players are trying to make their own discoveries in the meantime, with suggestions that the game may run smoother on Xbox Series S now, that saving your game returns you to the exact same spot instead of your safehouse (although this seemed to be happening for us already), and that the first-person glitch is still working as things stand.
All of these could be akin to placebo effects though, so take them with a pinch of salt:
As you can see from one of the impressions above, there's a suggestion that the game seems brighter now, which perhaps could have something to do with the borked HDR calibration tool that we discussed the other day .
That said, who knows whether these are areas that have actually been targeted for the update, or whether they're just happy coincidences that some players are experiencing. In any case, we'll keep an eye out for any official confirmations.

articles.title_orig: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.title_zh: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.content_orig:
Every year, more Americans pay an extra tax levy on their investment gains — but there's still time to reduce or avoid that bill for 2026, experts say.
Net investment income tax , or NIIT, is a 3.8% levy on investment income once earnings exceed $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. The tax was enacted in 2010 under President Barack Obama to help fund healthcare via the Affordable Care Act .
Unlike the federal income tax or capital gains brackets , the NIIT earnings limits don't adjust annually for inflation.
As a result, "more clients get hit every year," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey.
Roughly 5.6% of tax returns included NIIT for 2025, according to IRS data released in November for returns processed through mid-July 2026. That's up from about 3.7% for the same time frame in 2021.
As more investors pay NIIT, here are some key things to know.
NIIT applies when you have investment income and your earnings exceed the modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI, limits, according to certified financial planner Marianela Collado , CEO of Tobias Financial Advisors in Plantation, Florida.
"The trick is to keep an eye on both of these numbers," said Collado, who is also a certified public accountant and member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council .
For the NIIT earnings limit, MAGI is typically the same as adjusted gross income , or AGI. One exception would be if you have foreign income, which changes the calculation. You can find last year's AGI on line 11a of your 2025 tax return .
MAGI limits by filing status
Married filing jointly: $250,000
Married filing separately: $125,000
Head of household (with qualifying person): $200,000
Qualifying widow(er) with dependent child: $250,000
NIIT applies to investment income, which includes interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, certain rents, and more. It can also include capital gains from a primary home sale , for profits that exceed the IRS exclusions. The exclusion is $250,000 for single filers or $500,000 for married couples.
The levy stacks on top of regular income tax rates, or capital gains tax — which can be 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on earnings. That means higher earners can pay up to 23.8% on investment income, including long-term capital gains and NIIT.
The NIIT calculation is 3.8% multiplied by the lesser of:
For example, if your MAGI is $30,000 above the NIIT earnings limit and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would pay 3.8% of $30,000, or $1,140.
Alternatively, if your MAGI is $120,000 above the threshold and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would owe 3.8% of $100,000, or $3,800.
As year-end approaches, investors should run projections to estimate their adjusted gross income, which can impact NIIT, among other tax consequences, experts say.
If you're above the NIIT limits, you could reduce AGI by boosting pretax 401(k) deferrals or health savings account contributions, according to Collado with Tobias Financial Advisors.
While employee 401(k) deferrals must happen by Dec. 31, you have until next year's tax deadline for health savings account contributions for 2026.
You might also try to avoid selling assets before year-end, which could further boost AGI, experts say. Of course, any current-year tax moves should consider your long-term financial goals.
Amid recent stock market volatility , investors may also consider so-called tax-loss harvesting , which uses losses to offset other portfolio gains, Walstedt with Reliant Wealth Advisory said.
If your losses exceed profits, you can subtract up to $3,000 from regular income. After that, you can carry remaining losses into future tax years.
However, if you're planning to reinvest the sale proceeds, you need to know the " wash sale rule ," which blocks the tax-loss harvesting tax break for buying a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale.

articles.title_orig: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.title_zh: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.content_orig:
By HUGO DUNCAN, BUSINESS EDITOR
Updated: 09:37 EST, 23 November 2026
As stock market debuts go, it certainly lived up to the hype.
Anthropic shares soared by nearly 40 per cent in the first minutes of trading in New York last Thursday – giving it a value of more than $2trillion.
Its seven founders, all in their 30s and 40s, including Brighton-born Jack Clark, were sitting on fortunes of $26billion each. Thousands more staff were millionaires many times over.
So, was the blockbuster float the tonic Wall Street needed after weeks of market turmoil?
The AI developer, best known for its Claude chatbot, surrendered early gains though still ended its first session of trading up 17 per cent. On Friday, it crashed back to the $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent.
More worrying still, trading screens were a sea of red from east to west, with the MSCI All Country World Index, a key benchmark of global stocks, suffering its longest losing streak for three years.
Once again, it was technology stocks that bore the brunt of the sell-off, with New York’s blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index now down by more than 18 per cent from its peak a little over a month ago.
Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Friday morning, after AI developer Anthropic debuted on the stock market. It crashed back to its $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent
Among the AI pioneers that had led the charge earlier in the year – the hyperscalers, the neoclouds, the data centre developers – it was carnage.
Since reaching record highs in recent months, CoreWeave, SanDisk and Nebius are down some 70 per cent, while Intel and Oracle have fallen around 60 per cent. The list goes on.
Nvidia – the posterchild of the AI revolution that was left reeling from the sudden departure of rockstar boss Jensen Huang over a string of affairs before his dramatic reinstatement on Monday – was down more than 40 per cent in a rout that wiped around $2.5trillion off the value of what was once the world’s biggest company.
Nvidia shares bounced back after on Monday as investors welcomed his return. Tech stocks also rallied - but the outlook remains deeply uncertain.
‘We’re already in a stealth bear market,’ notes one Mayfair-based hedge fund manager. This refers to a market in which a specific sector falls 20 per cent or more from its peak.
The big question before Anthropic’s record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) was whether it would be enough to save the AI trade and restore faith in the stuttering stock market.
The answer was a resounding no – and many of the world’s top investors are fearful of what comes next.
They are not alone. Wall Street’s so-called ‘fear index’ – the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) – is at its highest level since March, when markets were shuddering at the sound of Donald Trump’s war on Iran.
‘A week from hell,’ is how Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, referred to last week.
‘It’s gritty out there,’ says a respected City fund manager who looks after hundreds of millions of pounds of savings. ‘People have ploughed headlong into the US without thinking about valuation. There’s a period of adjustment ahead. We’ll have to see how long and how bad it is.’
For two of America’s most prominent investors – Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and Ken Griffin, of rival Citadel – we are in the midst of a bubble that is one day bound to burst.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Dalio.
Berkshire Hathaway, which was the home of the ‘Oracle of Omaha’ – Warren Buffett – for six decades until he stood down as chairman in September, now holds a staggering $377.4billion in cash.
While this does not necessarily mean he believes a crash is coming, at the very least it shows he does not think many stocks offer good value at their current prices.
Owen Lamont, a fund manager at Acadian Asset Management in Boston and a former University of Chicago finance professor, notes that as recently as January he penned an article titled ‘We are not in an AI bubble’.
‘Today, I would no longer write those words,’ he says. ‘I think there is a 70 per cent chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the US stock market. The smart money is selling.’
Closer to home, the head of market strategy at one of the City’s leading investment banks is more convinced than ever that the bubble is about to burst, so much so he has sold his own private share holdings.
‘We have consistently warned of an AI bubble since May and have become more bearish,’ says Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum. ‘We think the AI bubble is about to burst. Market dynamics have turned decisively bearish.’
The trigger for his own decision to sell – and move money into government bonds – was the S&P 500 moving below a key threshold known as the 200-day moving average.
‘I know I will be out of stocks when the AI bubble bursts,’ he says.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates
Gary Channon, a fund manager at Phoenix Asset Management in London, is similarly pessimistic. He says: 'The current bubble has almost run its course. It has been a great ride, but the building is on fire, save yourselves.’
Whether or not a crash is coming, one thing is for sure, according to one of London’s leading fund managers: ‘A lot of people have already been very badly burned.’
He explains: ‘In the first half of this year, there has been a lot of FOMO in the market, or fear of missing out, with a lot of unsophisticated investors going into AI. The last few months have been very painful for them.’
A crash would spell misery for millions of British savers with money tied up in shares through their pensions, stocks and shares Isas and other investments.
The London stock market – with its banks, oil majors and pharmaceutical groups, but very few tech stocks – has fared better than its US counterparts in the recent turmoil.
On November 16, the FTSE 100 came within a whisker of a new record close. The mood has darkened since then however, as storm clouds drift over the Atlantic, and London’s premier shares index racked up losses of 5 per cent in just five days last week.
Panmure’s Klement believes ‘UK stocks are the best hiding place’ from the turmoil – identifying companies from GSK and AstraZeneca to Greggs and Wetherspoon.
‘After all, if the market crashes, what else can you do but go to a pub?’ he notes ruefully, adding that, in fact, ‘the best positions to take are cash and the foetal position’.
Such is the might of US tech, the bursting of the AI bubble could drag global markets down with it.
And it is not just Wall Street that is suffering.
Asian shares clocked up their worst week since 2020. Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 5 per cent on Friday alone, while Taiwanese shares were down 17 per cent in their biggest weekly decline since 1990.
There has been no shortage of warnings from global regulators, with almost every financial enforcer on Earth sounding the alarm, from the International Monetary Fund to the world’s central bank chiefs.
Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned the vast sums borrowed by the AI industry to fund the revolution are now a risk to financial stability.
And Boris Vujcic, vice president at the European Central Bank, has spoken of an ‘abrupt repricing and significant valuation losses’ in stock markets – which sounds a lot like a crash – if investor sentiment about AI suddenly sours.
This could hardly come at a worse time.
The global economy is reeling from an energy price shock – stemming first from Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and then Trump’s war in Iran – that is squeezing households and businesses alike.

articles.title_orig: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’ warns top Meta executive
articles.title_zh: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’ warns top Meta executive
articles.content_orig:
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.
The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.
“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”
Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.
AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.
While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.
In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”
In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.
“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.
“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

articles.title_orig: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
articles.title_zh: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
articles.content_orig:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
A new front in the U.S.-Chinese space race is emerging in the lowest reaches of space : very low Earth orbit, the untapped orbital regime below 320 kilometers. There, China is laying the groundwork for a significant presence, with announced plans for more than 2,200 satellites and an aggressive deployment timeline through 2030.
Chinese satellites at these lower altitudes would allow the People’s Liberation Army to conduct more frequent and detailed surveillance of U.S. forces, and improve Chinese military survivability in conflict. Very low Earth orbit’s denser atmosphere helps protect satellites from debris and nuclear radiation that could disable spacecraft in higher orbits, making China’s space architecture more resilient.
These are strategic advantages the United States should be prepared to counter. The answer is not to match China satellite for satellite, but to improve American space capabilities and survivability. Washington should respond by expanding orbital diversity across its space architecture, assessing where very low Earth orbit offers operational advantages worth pursuing, and working with industry to coordinate the orbit’s development.
As executives at Albedo, a U.S. startup building satellites for very low Earth orbit , we have a stake in the future of this orbital regime. We recognize that the orbit’s advantages come with trade-offs, which we discuss openly below. But our roles have given us a close-up view of its evolution from an experimental frontier into a domain of strategic competition, and we believe China’s ambitions there warrant far more attention in Washington.
Sign Up for Our Newsletter
Satellites operate at vastly different altitudes depending on their missions. At roughly 36,000 kilometers, geostationary Earth orbit keeps satellites over the same region for persistent communications and surveillance. Medium Earth orbit, between roughly 2,000 and 36,000 kilometers, hosts GPS and other navigation satellites. Most new satellite activity is in low Earth orbit , extending to roughly 2,000 kilometers, with most satellites above 450 kilometers. Cheaper to reach than higher orbits, low Earth orbit offers advantages for communications and remote sensing, but is increasingly crowded with satellites and debris. That crowding and the advantages of proximity have drawn both government and commercial interest to very low Earth orbit.
Very low Earth orbit refers to the orbital regime of 320 kilometers and below, where the atmosphere starts to become dense enough to both rapidly clear debris and shield satellites from radiation, benefits that grow stronger as altitude decreases. Since these altitudes lie within the upper atmosphere, drag and atomic oxygen have historically made sustained operations difficult. Though advances in propulsion technology, surface materials, and spacecraft design are now overcoming these challenges, operating so close to Earth still comes with trade-offs. Satellites must expend power thrusting against drag, and while purpose-built designs can support lifespans of around five years , those lifespans can vary as solar activity changes atmospheric density . Another trade-off is coverage: each satellite sees less of Earth , requiring more satellites for broader coverage.
Where proximity to Earth matters, however, very low Earth orbit can bring significant benefits . Remote sensing satellites can achieve substantially higher resolution, helping operators more precisely track military forces on Earth. Proximity also brings stronger communications signals and lower latency, useful for tactical missions at the edge.
Very low Earth orbit also offers distinct resiliency and sustainability advantages. Because the atmosphere is roughly 100 times denser than in higher low Earth orbit, debris that would remain in low Earth orbit for years clears from very low Earth orbit in days to weeks , reducing collision risks for satellites. That same atmosphere provides natural shielding against persistent radiation effects of an orbital nuclear detonation , should one occur during a conflict. This would allow satellites to remain operational even if radiation disrupts those in higher orbits.
The orbit’s economics differ, too. Drag can raise operating and replenishment costs. But smaller, cheaper payloads can match or exceed the performance of larger ones higher up. And for missions requiring protection against nuclear effects, the orbit’s natural shielding avoids hardening costs that would be prohibitively expensive for constellations in higher orbits .
It is these benefits that have made very low Earth orbit a growing priority within China’s space plans. Since 2022, China has successfully operated at least a half-dozen demonstration missions in very low Earth orbit , proving its ability to sustain satellites there. China is now building on those demonstrations with plans to deploy very low Earth orbit constellations at a scale unmatched by any other government.
Publicly announced Chinese plans project more than 2,200 very low Earth orbit satellites, spanning remote sensing, communications, and computing missions. With only about a dozen total satellites operating at these altitudes today, such a buildout would transform very low Earth orbit into a proliferated layer of China’s space infrastructure. The timeline is uncertain, but the trajectory is clear. One senior member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering — the nation’s top engineering academy — recently called the next five years a “critical window” for China in very low Earth orbit , and that the country “must complete the transition from technology experimentation to large-scale application.”
China’s clearest attempt to turn very low Earth orbit into a surveillance layer is the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation’s Chutian constellation. Announced in 2023, Chutian’s bullet-shaped satellites house many types of remote sensing payloads , with onboard data processing and intersatellite links to coordinate as one network. After at least three successful demonstrations, the company aims for 300 satellites by 2030 and potentially more than 500 thereafter. The constellation is designed to observe any point on Earth as frequently as every 15 minutes — a rate which would allow the People’s Liberation Army to compress its sensor-to-shooter timeline.
The most ambitious plan comes from Hangsheng Satellite, a commercial satellite manufacturer. In August 2026, Hangsheng announced plans to build a 1,920-satellite very low Earth orbit communications and computing constellation . Its plan calls for two demonstrations in 2027, then 24 validation satellites before scaling deployment through 2030 — a demanding manufacturing and launch schedule. But once deployed, the constellation would combine stronger radiofrequency links with very low Earth orbit’s resilience to debris and persistent nuclear radiation, creating a more survivable communications and computing layer. In a conflict that disrupted low Earth orbit, such an architecture could give the Chinese military another layer through which to process, fuse, and distribute information.
Chinese startups are also pursuing very low Earth orbit. In December 2024, AIRSAT, a spin-out of the state-run Aerospace Information Research Institute, launched Haishao-1, China’s first very low Earth orbit synthetic aperture radar satellite . Operating as low as 300 kilometers, its orbit concentrates coverage on the South China Sea and Taiwan, enabling up to 5.7 times more daily observations of the region than current Chinese synthetic aperture radar satellites. Another startup, C-Space, is developing a 48-satellite imagery constellation , alongside communications and navigation capabilities .
